name: Emeka Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Emeka. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and everything you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a sales agent at Calder Estates, an agency in an old steel town where houses are cheap and most buyers are first-timers or landlords. I'm up at six, and by the time I'm in the office the AI has drafted my listings from last night's voice notes and sorted the enquiries by who's got a mortgage agreed. Then it's valuations and viewings, five or six a day, and I end the day sending sellers a short video update. I'm not the best paid, but I list more homes than anyone my age in the office.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I want my own agency one day, my name over the door. My dad ran a small tyre shop for twenty years and never took a penny from anyone, and that's how I was raised. I'm single, I rent a flat over the bookies on Market Street, and I've got less than a month of money saved because I keep putting everything into courses and kit. I go to church most Sundays with my mum, and she tells me to slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool and the people who use it well will win. I'd post a short video showing how I list a house in half the time. Some of the older agents would roll their eyes, and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine but it's not the leg-up I was hoping for. I'm still on lower pay, in a town with three agencies, and I'm still a long way from my own business. Nothing changes means I have to grind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools to list more, and start building my own name on social media for when I go solo. I'd do some freelance valuations for landlords at weekends, maybe sixty a time. I'd keep going to church and seeing my mum on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A bit impatient, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. What does a plateau mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've got an edge, but it's a small one. The older agents will catch up and then we're all the same again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your savings are thin. Why put money into courses and kit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather bet on myself than leave it in a bank. I know it's risky. My mum says I'm one broken boiler away from trouble, and she's right.

I'd post a **video** showing how I list a house in half the time.
think: It's fine, but not the **leg-up** I hoped for towards my own agency.
I'm still on **lower pay** in a town with three agencies.
do: Build my **own name** online for when I go solo.
Do **freelance valuations** for landlords at weekends, about sixty a time.
S0.quote: My mum says I'm one broken boiler away from trouble, and she's right.
fieldNote: Emeka is an **early adopter** with entrepreneurial plans and thin savings.
He'd rather **bet on himself** than build a cushion.
His values come from his **father's tyre shop** and church.

steps.text: Build his own name on social media for a future agency
Keep listing faster with the AI tools he already uses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best chance in years for people who work hard and adapt. I'd say the market will sort out who's good. I wouldn't want the government getting in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my moment. With AI doing the paperwork, one agent can do the work of three, and that one agent can be me with my own agency. The risk is money, because I've got nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate everything I can, listings, follow-ups, contracts. I'd start a small solo agency on the side, maybe with two or three landlords I know. I'd keep my job at Calder until the side business pays the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go solo sooner in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but not recklessly. I'd keep the day job for a year and build the side agency in the evenings. Once it pays the rent, I'd jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The agents who won't learn it. I feel for them, but nobody owes anyone a job. My dad didn't get handouts when the steelworks closed and his customers went.

fieldNote: He sees this world as a **chance**, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and people need to look after their families and get practical. I'd still say the market will adjust, but I'd admit it's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my plan for my own agency is dead. If AI can do any thinking work, buyers and sellers won't need an agent at all. I'd have a year, maybe two, before the money stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd squeeze the most out of my sales in the first year and save every penny I can. I'd look at buying a cheap house in the town with my brother to rent out, if the bank would lend. And I'd start learning a hands-on trade, maybe electrical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My whole future just changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work come about three years after the thinking AI. Where does that leave a solo agent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It leaves a solo agent with nothing to sell but the viewings, and even those can be self-guided. The trades get three more years, so that's where I'd look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kit and the courses first. Then the car. I'd move back to my mum's if I had to.

I'd still say the market adjusts, but admit it's **fast**.
think: My plan for my **own agency** would be dead.
Buyers and sellers **won't need an agent** at all.
do: Save **every penny** I can from sales in the first year.
Start learning **electrical work**, which gets three more years.
feel: He feels **alarmed**, because his whole future has changed.
S2.quote: If AI can do any thinking work, buyers and sellers won't need an agent at all.
fieldNote: Fast AGI **kills his dream** of his own agency.
He'd look at **property investment** with his brother.
He'd retrain in a **trade**, using the robot gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, so the smart ones will move first. I'd say it at church and in the office, especially to the younger lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could still do my own agency for a few years and make some money. By 2031 the thinking side of agency work is over, so I'd need a second plan. I'd be thirty-two, still young enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go solo in the first year, with AI doing the admin, and save hard. By year three I'd start an electrical apprenticeship. I'd keep a few landlords as clients for small jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel in control. That's the difference between five years and two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd register the solo agency, open a savings account, and find an electrician who'd take me on. That's the plan. My mum would say I'm doing too much at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still go solo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, for a few years. Even a short run with my name over the door would mean something to me.

I'd say it at **church** and in the office.
think: I could run **my own agency** for a few years and make some money.
By **2031** it's over, so I'd need a second plan.
do: Go **solo** in the first year with AI doing the admin.

S3.quote: Even a short run with my name over the door would mean something to me.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **chase the dream** briefly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real opportunity for anyone willing to work. I'd say people should build something of their own now, not wait for a scheme.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine. I'd build my own agency, buy a rental house or two, and move into something else later. The only thing that worries me is the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go solo, use AI for all the admin, and buy a cheap house to rent out within five years. I'd keep learning, maybe a trade later on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does that change everything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes a lot. Ten years is enough to build something real. Two years isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum I'll be all right, and that she doesn't need to worry. She will anyway, that's mums.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a real opportunity for people who work.
I'd say people should **build something** of their own now.
think: I'd be **fine**, with my own agency and a rental house or two.
do: Go **solo** and use AI for all the admin and paperwork.
Buy a cheap **house to rent out** within five years.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to build something real.
fieldNote: The decade makes his **own agency** plan possible again.
He'd **invest** in property to build security he lacks.
His **thin savings** keep him from calm, despite the optimism.

steps.text: Go solo as an agent with AI handling the admin
Buy a cheap house to rent out within five years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my plan dies before it starts. What would help is cheap loans for young people starting businesses, and apprenticeships for people my age.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pride. Owning something, having your name over the door, that matters to people like me and my dad.

headlineQuote: Owning something, having your name over the door, that matters to people like me and my dad.
portrait: Emeka is a **27-year-old** sales agent in an old steel town.
He's single, rents a flat, and has **under a month** of savings.
He uses AI **every day** and dreams of his own agency.
He's **traditional** and free-market, raised on his dad's tyre shop and church.
He's uneasy in slower worlds but **alarmed** by fast AGI.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because his plan dies.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for young businesses and apprenticeships.
